title.text: Cost Segregation for a Prior-Year Property: How to Catch Up with Form 3115

data.excerpt: Purchased a rental or commercial property several years ago without completing cost segregation? Don’t worry – you can likely still save tens of thousands on your taxes.

body.text: By Amar Patel | Principal, Cost Segregation
Purchased a rental or commercial property several years ago without completing cost segregation? Don’t worry – you can likely still save tens of thousands on your taxes.

This is because when it comes to taxes, a building is really a collection of assets purchased together. The structure can last for decades, while appliances, flooring, landscaping, and parking areas wear out much sooner. Cost segregation, often called cost seg, separates qualifying components and places them on shorter depreciation schedules instead of leaving nearly everything on the building’s 27.5- or 39-year timeline. For more info, IRS Publication 946 explains the full federal depreciation framework.

For a property already in service, cost segregation becomes a look-back process. The report rebuilds the property’s depreciation history from the date it became ready to rent or use, then compares what the investor should have claimed with what they actually deducted. That difference gives the CPA the information needed to evaluate a Section 481(a) catch-up adjustment and prepare Form 3115.

CostSegregation.com turns these steps into a guided online process. For eligible properties, the software generates the property-specific cost segregation report, updated depreciation schedules, and a Section 481(a) calculation schedule when applicable. The investor can invite their CPA into the workflow, and the CPA uses those materials to review and prepare the filing.
Key Takeaways
Cost segregation remains available for eligible properties that an investor purchased, constructed, or placed in service in a prior year.
A look-back report calculates what the depreciation history should have been and compares it with the deductions already claimed.
CostSegregation.com creates the property analysis and Section 481(a) schedule that the investor’s CPA needs to begin the Form 3115 process.
Cost Segregation Still Works After the First Year

The easiest time to complete cost segregation is usually when a property is purchased, constructed, or significantly improved. That timing lets the investor begin using the accelerated deductions from the start.
Missing that first-year opportunity does not erase it. A look-back cost seg report returns to the property’s original placed-in-service date: the date it became ready and available to rent or use.

The report begins with the original building basis after land is removed. It then identifies the property components that belonged on shorter 5-, 7-, or 15-year schedules and recalculates the depreciation through the beginning of the current tax year.
This creates a clear comparison:
Depreciation the investor already claimed
Depreciation the investor should have claimed
The difference represents the potential catch-up adjustment.
What Your CPA Needs for Form 3115

Form 3115 reports certain changes in accounting method. In a qualifying look-back situation, the form allows the investor to correct the depreciation treatment without rewriting several years of tax returns one at a time.

The Section 481(a) adjustment measures the cumulative difference between the depreciation actually deducted and the amount allowable before the year of change. A negative adjustment generally reduces taxable income in the current year.

The CPA cannot calculate that amount from the purchase price alone. The filing requires the underlying property analysis, corrected classifications, depreciation schedules, and prior-year comparison. That is where the completed cost segregation report becomes essential.
The exact filing approach depends on the property’s depreciation history and the applicable accounting-method procedures. The CPA reviews the report and determines how Form 3115 applies.

faqs.question: Do I Need to Amend Every Prior Tax Return?

answer.text: Often, no. When an accounting method change applies, the CPA generally uses Form 3115 and a Section 481(a) adjustment instead of amending each prior-year return. The property’s depreciation history determines the correct filing path.

faqs.question: Can short-term rental owners use CostSegregation.com?

answer.text: Yes. Short-term rental owners may use CostSegregation.com when the property qualifies. Cost segregation can be especially valuable for short-term rentals because they often include assets that qualify for shorter depreciation periods. A cost seg report also supports the accelerated-depreciation portion of the STR loophole strategy. Average-stay, material-participation, and other requirements should be reviewed with a tax advisor.
